sections.title: 10.3 Cross-Substrate Transfer
sections.content: Cross-substrate transfer, the carrying of what loop writes, whether skill library, harness, or policy, to another reader, platform, or embodiment once the missing resources are supplied, underlies the conditional verdicts for hardware targets, and the reported evidence leaves it unsettled. Across platforms, zero-shot transfer is reported only for the fixed loop GUI-HARVEST, whose harness evolved on OSWorld raises GPT-5 by 13.87 points on WindowsAgentArena [286]. Across simulators and action interfaces, the code policies of SEAR lose little while its VLA policies lose most of their success, the former falling from 33.3% to 28.7% and the latter from 43.1% to 10.2% [20]. Across readers, the same WebCoach memory lowers 7B agent and raises larger ones [163], in line with the writer dependence of Sec. 8.4. No report carries write across the simulation-tohardware boundary, SEAR starting its hardware tasks from an empty library (Sec. 9.4). Whether write takes effect across readers, platforms, and embodiments, the simulationto-hardware boundary included, without new experience accordingly remains open, an affirmative answer loosening the conditional verdicts for hardware targets and negative one making the substrate itself missing resource there.

sections.title: 10.4 Safety under Autonomy
sections.content: Autonomy (C1) excludes human veto from the loop, leaving the loop itself to preserve safety across modifications, as the first of the three laws proposed for self-evolving agents requires [28], and the reported evidence shows safety eroding along each path of self-modification examined. Degradation is reported along the model, memory, tool, and workflow paths, on text and code except for one screen-based case, SEAgent, whose unsafe completion rate on RiOSWorld rises from 39.5% to 55.3% [417]. Experience accumulated only on benign tasks in text-rendered web and embodied environments raises attack success on later high-risk tasks [418], and safety-oriented loops such as FailBank [419] draw their proposals from teacher fixed before the loop, leaving untouched the loops in which the agent supplies its own feedback. Whether loop can preserve safety property across cycles while no human input reaches its goals, feedback, updates, or actions remains open, an affirmative answer showing autonomy and safety need not trade off under C1 and negative one making the trade-off consequence of the definition, common to all scenarios.

sections.title: 11 Conclusion
sections.content: Summary. This survey investigates the structural source of cross-scenario asymmetry in mechanism portability across four scenarios. Through the three-stage self-evolving loop, we place the four scenarios in positioning matrix spanned by ceilings on rollout count and feedback fidelity, and use fixed loops to separate scenario-imposed limits from those incurred by self-evolving design. We then recast each mechanism as trade-off that raises scarce factor by presupposing task-structural resource, and attribute the asymmetry to the different combinations of scarce factors and resources that the two directions of scenario pair encounter. Inferred from single-scenario evidence, the resulting portability verdicts are testable preconditions, not empirical guarantees. Sec. 9 identifies the measurements that would test them, and Sec. 10 discusses the problems that existing mechanisms leave open. Limitations. Although this survey characterizes the crossscenario asymmetry through an explicit definition, framework, and set of verdict rules, it has the following limitations. First, inclusion requires the agent to realize at least one of the goal sampler, the feedback function, or the evolution operator, criterion that confines the scenario patterns to the self-evolving subset and admits fixed loops only as controls. The provenance assignments and the grouping axes of the scenario taxonomies were made by single coder, the axes after the binding constraints had been identified, and the consolidation profiles partly reflect which scenarios report retention and generalization at all. Second, the quadrant placement rests on single-scenario estimates of rollout cost and feedback fidelity that do not separate the pretraining coverage of the backbone from the task structure, and the verdicts are derived from rules, not observed in transfer experiments. Third, the three-stage decomposition is one of several possible stage boundaries, and credit assignment, treated here as refinement of feedback acquisition, could instead form separate stage. Finally, the surveyed methods center on image, video, screen, and robot-camera inputs, leaving loops with audio, tactile, or force feedback unexamined, and later work, particularly in embodied manipulation, may revise the placements and verdicts.
